title: Money laundering isn't named after Al Capone 🧺
description:
The story says Al Capone hid his cash in laundromats and gave us the term "money laundering". Probably a myth: in 1910 the US Treasury literally washed dirty banknotes (a machine cleaned and pressed about 25,000 a day), while the criminal sense of the word shows up in print around 1970 and went mainstream with Watergate in 1973. Capone himself was convicted of income tax evasion in 1931: 11 years, part of it on Alcatraz.

Sources: Mental Floss (the Capone myth); History Today (the Treasury's money-washing machine); Word Origins (earliest uses of the term); US National Archives (U.S. v. Alphonse Capone).

meta.topic: the Al Capone laundromat myth: the Treasury literally washed banknotes from 1910 (~25,000/day), the criminal term appears ~1970 and spreads with Watergate (1973); what laundering means; Capone convicted of tax evasion 1931 (11 years, Alcatraz)
meta.idea_source: unique + viral-shaped: a famous gangster myth most people repeat, busted with a literal money-washing machine; the channel's first dark-files Short (owner's new format)

humour.trend: 'left on read' slang (still in daily use) as a side-eye card about Capone's tax return

claims.claim: the Capone-laundromat origin of the term is most likely a myth
1910: a Treasury (Bureau of Engraving and Printing) machine cleaned and pressed ~25,000 notes a day
criminal 'launder' in print by 1970 (Globe and Mail); popularised by Watergate reporting in 1973
Capone never paid income tax (1925-1929 indictment); guilty Oct 1931; 11 years, 4.5 of 7.5 served on Alcatraz

speaker: ved

scenes.say: Money laundering, named after Capone's *laundromats*? Probably a myth.
